```{r}
#| label: load-packages
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(knitr)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
credit <- read_csv("data/Credit_Update.csv") |>
  clean_names() |>
  select(!x1) |>
  remove_empty()
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-inline-values
n_total        <- nrow(credit)
n_vars         <- ncol(credit)
n_caucasian    <- credit |> filter(ethnicity == "Caucasian") |> nrow()
pct_caucasian  <- round(n_caucasian / n_total * 100, 1)
n_asian        <- credit |> filter(ethnicity == "Asian") |> nrow()
pct_asian      <- round(n_asian / n_total * 100, 1)
n_african      <- credit |> filter(ethnicity == "African American") |> nrow()
pct_african    <- round(n_african / n_total * 100, 1)
n_female       <- credit |> filter(gender == "Female") |> nrow()
pct_female     <- round(n_female / n_total * 100, 1)
n_student      <- credit |> filter(student == "Yes") |> nrow()
pct_student    <- round(n_student / n_total * 100, 1)
n_married      <- credit |> filter(married == "Yes") |> nrow()
pct_married    <- round(n_married / n_total * 100, 1)
med_income     <- round(median(credit$income, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
mean_income    <- round(mean(credit$income, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
med_balance    <- round(median(credit$balance, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
mean_balance   <- round(mean(credit$balance, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
cor_lim_bal    <- round(cor(credit$limit, credit$balance), 3)
cor_inc_bal    <- round(cor(credit$income, credit$balance), 3)
cor_rat_bal    <- round(cor(credit$rating, credit$balance), 3)
```

# Introduction

This report presents a descriptive analysis of credit card holder data drawn from the 2026 quarterly credit report. The dataset captures financial and demographic characteristics of `{r} n_total` cardholders, including income, credit limit, credit rating, outstanding balance, and personal background.

The purpose of this report is to describe the profile of cardholders, understand the distribution of credit balances, and identify the financial variables most associated with higher credit card balances. The findings are intended to support informed decision-making for credit management and portfolio review.

# Background

Credit card balance — the outstanding amount owed on a credit card — is a key indicator of credit utilization and financial exposure for both cardholders and lenders. Understanding which factors are associated with higher balances helps identify patterns in borrowing behavior and informs risk assessment.

Several financial variables are expected to play a role. Credit limit and credit rating are direct measures of a cardholder's credit standing and are likely to be closely linked to balance levels. Income, while not directly controlling credit issuance, reflects a cardholder's repayment capacity and may be moderately associated with balance. Demographic characteristics — including age, education, gender, ethnicity, and student or marital status — provide context for understanding the diversity of the cardholder population.

This analysis focuses on describing these variables and examining their relationship to credit card balance.

# Method

## Data source

The dataset, `Credit_Update.csv`, was obtained from the quarterly credit reporting system (2026). It contains records for `{r} n_total` credit card holders and `{r} n_vars` variables covering financial metrics and demographic attributes.

## Variables

The variables used in this analysis are described in @tbl-variables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-variables
#| tbl-cap: "Description of variables in the dataset"
tibble(
  Variable    = c("Income", "Limit", "Rating", "Cards", "Age",
                  "Education", "Gender", "Student", "Married",
                  "Ethnicity", "Balance"),
  Type        = c("Numeric", "Integer", "Integer", "Integer", "Integer",
                  "Integer", "Categorical", "Categorical", "Categorical",
                  "Categorical", "Integer"),
  Description = c(
    "Annual income in thousands of US dollars",
    "Credit card limit in US dollars",
    "Credit rating score",
    "Number of credit cards held",
    "Age of the cardholder in years",
    "Years of formal education completed",
    "Male or Female",
    "Whether the cardholder is a student (Yes / No)",
    "Whether the cardholder is married (Yes / No)",
    "Ethnic group: African American, Asian, or Caucasian",
    "Average monthly credit card balance in US dollars"
  )
) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Variable", "Type", "Description"))
```

## Data preparation

The raw CSV file was imported using the `readr` package. The unnamed row-index column was removed, column names were standardized to lowercase `snake_case` using the `janitor` package, and empty rows and columns were dropped. No missing values were identified in any column following this cleaning step.

## Analytical approach

The analysis proceeds in two stages. First, a demographic profile of the cardholder population is constructed using frequency counts and percentages for categorical variables, and summary statistics (mean, median, standard deviation) for numeric variables. Second, the key analysis examines the distribution of credit card balance and its association with financial and demographic variables using summary tables and visualizations.

All analyses were conducted in R using the `tidyverse` suite of packages. Visualizations were produced with `ggplot2`.

# Results

## Demographic profile

### Sample overview

The dataset comprises `{r} n_total` cardholders. @tbl-demographics summarizes the categorical demographic characteristics.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Demographic profile of cardholders"
bind_rows(
  credit |>
    count(Category = ethnicity) |>
    mutate(Group = "Ethnicity", Percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)),
  credit |>
    count(Category = gender) |>
    mutate(Group = "Gender", Percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)),
  credit |>
    count(Category = student) |>
    mutate(Group = "Student status", Percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)),
  credit |>
    count(Category = married) |>
    mutate(Group = "Marital status", Percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))
) |>
  select(Group, Category, n, Percent) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Category", "Count", "Percent (%)"))
```

Caucasian cardholders represent the largest ethnic group (`{r} n_caucasian` of `{r} n_total`, `{r} pct_caucasian`%), followed closely by Asian (`{r} pct_asian`%) and African American cardholders (`{r} pct_african`%). The sample is nearly evenly split by gender, with females comprising `{r} pct_female`% of cardholders. The majority of cardholders are non-students (`{r} 100 - pct_student`%) and married (`{r} pct_married`%).

@fig-bar-demographics provides a visual overview of the sample composition by ethnicity.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar-demographics
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of cardholders by ethnic group"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
credit |>
  count(ethnicity) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1),
         label = paste0(n, " (", pct, "%)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(ethnicity, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  ylim(0, 240) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of cardholders",
    caption = "Data source: Credit_Update.csv, 2026"
  )
```

### Numeric variable summary

@tbl-numeric-summary presents descriptive statistics for the continuous variables in the dataset.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-numeric-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for numeric variables"
credit |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(income, limit, rating, balance, age, education, cards),
      list(
        Mean   = \(x) round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
        Median = \(x) round(median(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
        SD     = \(x) round(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
        Min    = \(x) min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
        Max    = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to  = c("Variable", "Statistic"),
    names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Statistic, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(Variable = str_to_title(Variable)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Variable", "Mean", "Median", "SD", "Min", "Max"))
```

Annual income ranges from approximately \$10,000 to \$187,000, with a median of \$`{r} med_income`K. The mean (\$`{r} mean_income`K) is notably higher than the median, indicating that the income distribution is right-skewed — a small number of high earners pull the mean upward. The average credit card balance is \$`{r} mean_balance`, with a median of \$`{r} med_balance`, again reflecting a right-skewed distribution.

## Key analysis

### Distribution of income

@fig-hist-income shows the distribution of annual income. The distribution is strongly right-skewed, with the majority of cardholders earning below \$60,000 annually and a long tail extending toward higher earners.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist-income
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of annual income (in $1,000s). The dashed lines indicate the median (red) and mean (black)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(credit, aes(x = income)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(credit$income), color = "red",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(credit$income), color = "black",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = median(credit$income) - 2, y = 28,
           label = paste0("Median = $", med_income, "K"),
           color = "red", hjust = 1, size = 3.3) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(credit$income) + 2, y = 28,
           label = paste0("Mean = $", mean_income, "K"),
           color = "black", hjust = 0, size = 3.3) +
  labs(
    x = "Annual income ($1,000s)",
    y = "Count",
    caption = "Data source: Credit_Update.csv, 2026"
  )
```

### Distribution of credit card balance

@fig-hist-balance shows the distribution of credit card balance. A notable number of cardholders carry a zero balance — these are cardholders who pay off their balance in full each month. Among those who do carry a balance, the distribution is broadly spread, with some cardholders approaching the upper limit of \$2,000.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist-balance
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of credit card balance (USD). The dashed lines indicate the median (red) and mean (black)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(credit, aes(x = balance)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(credit$balance), color = "red",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(credit$balance), color = "black",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = median(credit$balance) - 20, y = 37,
           label = paste0("Median = $", med_balance),
           color = "red", hjust = 1, size = 3.3) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(credit$balance) + 20, y = 37,
           label = paste0("Mean = $", mean_balance),
           color = "black", hjust = 0, size = 3.3) +
  labs(
    x = "Credit card balance (USD)",
    y = "Count",
    caption = "Data source: Credit_Update.csv, 2026"
  )
```

### Relationship between financial variables and balance

Credit limit and credit rating are the variables most strongly associated with credit card balance (@fig-scatter-limit-balance). The correlation between limit and balance is `{r} cor_lim_bal`, and between rating and balance is `{r} cor_rat_bal`, both indicating a strong positive relationship. Cardholders with higher credit limits and ratings tend to carry higher balances.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter-limit-balance
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between credit limit and credit card balance, by ethnicity"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(credit, aes(x = limit, y = balance, color = ethnicity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Credit limit (USD)",
    y = "Credit card balance (USD)",
    color = "Ethnicity",
    caption = "Data source: Credit_Update.csv, 2026"
  )
```

Income shows a moderate positive association with balance (r = `{r} cor_inc_bal`). As seen in @fig-scatter-income-balance, the relationship between income and balance is weaker than that of credit limit, and is consistent across ethnic groups.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter-income-balance
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between annual income and credit card balance, by ethnicity"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(credit, aes(x = income, y = balance, color = ethnicity)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Annual income ($1,000s)",
    y = "Credit card balance (USD)",
    color = "Ethnicity",
    caption = "Data source: Credit_Update.csv, 2026"
  )
```

### Balance by demographic group

@tbl-balance-by-group presents mean and median credit card balance broken down by key demographic categories.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-balance-by-group
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and median credit card balance by demographic group"
bind_rows(
  credit |>
    group_by(Category = ethnicity) |>
    summarise(
      Group  = "Ethnicity",
      n      = n(),
      Mean   = round(mean(balance), 0),
      Median = round(median(balance), 0)
    ),
  credit |>
    group_by(Category = gender) |>
    summarise(
      Group  = "Gender",
      n      = n(),
      Mean   = round(mean(balance), 0),
      Median = round(median(balance), 0)
    ),
  credit |>
    group_by(Category = student) |>
    summarise(
      Group  = "Student status",
      n      = n(),
      Mean   = round(mean(balance), 0),
      Median = round(median(balance), 0)
    ),
  credit |>
    group_by(Category = married) |>
    summarise(
      Group  = "Marital status",
      n      = n(),
      Mean   = round(mean(balance), 0),
      Median = round(median(balance), 0)
    )
) |>
  select(Group, Category, n, Mean, Median) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Category", "N", "Mean balance (\\$)", "Median balance (\\$)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-student-balance
student_mean    <- credit |> filter(student == "Yes") |> summarise(m = round(mean(balance), 0)) |> pull(m)
nonstudent_mean <- credit |> filter(student == "No")  |> summarise(m = round(mean(balance), 0)) |> pull(m)
```

Average credit card balance is broadly similar across ethnic groups, ranging from \$512 (Asian) to \$531 (African American). By gender, balances are also comparable. The most notable difference is by student status: student cardholders carry a mean balance of \$`{r} student_mean`, compared to \$`{r} nonstudent_mean` for non-student cardholders, suggesting that students tend to carry higher relative balances despite their smaller share of the sample.

@fig-balance-student illustrates the difference in balance distributions between student and non-student cardholders.

```{r}
#| label: fig-balance-student
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of credit card balance by student status"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(credit, aes(x = student, y = balance)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.4) +
  labs(
    x = "Student status",
    y = "Credit card balance (USD)",
    caption = "Data source: Credit_Update.csv, 2026"
  )
```

# Conclusion and discussion

This report provides a descriptive profile of `{r} n_total` credit card holders based on the 2026 quarterly credit data. The key findings are as follows.

The cardholder population is demographically diverse, with Caucasian cardholders forming a plurality (`{r} pct_caucasian`%) alongside Asian (`{r} pct_asian`%) and African American (`{r} pct_african`%) groups. The sample is approximately gender-balanced, predominantly non-student, and mostly married.

Income in this population is right-skewed, with a median of \$`{r} med_income`K and a mean pulled upward to \$`{r} mean_income`K by a smaller number of high earners. This skewness is an important consideration when summarizing this variable: the median provides a more representative picture of typical income than the mean.

The strongest predictor of credit card balance in this dataset is credit limit (r = `{r} cor_lim_bal`), followed closely by credit rating (r = `{r} cor_rat_bal`). Both reflect the lender's assessment of a cardholder's creditworthiness and directly shape the upper bound of borrowing. Income has a moderate association with balance (r = `{r} cor_inc_bal`), indicating that higher earners tend to carry larger balances, though the relationship is less direct.

Across ethnic groups and genders, average balances are similar — the data do not show meaningful differences by these demographic categories alone. The most notable demographic contrast is by student status: student cardholders carry substantially higher average balances than their non-student counterparts, which may reflect different spending needs or repayment behaviors and warrants closer monitoring.

This analysis is descriptive in nature. Observed associations — particularly between credit limit and balance — should not be interpreted as causal without further investigation. Future analysis could examine multivariate models to isolate the independent contribution of each variable, and could investigate the subset of cardholders with a zero balance separately from those who actively carry debt.
